slides.heading: Four Number Sum
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Four Number Sum, a hard arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: All quadruplets of distinct integers summing to target (any order).
Store pair sums seen before index i, combine with pairs after i, so each quadruplet is reported once.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. All quadruplets of distinct integers summing to target (any order). Store pair sums seen before index i, combine with pairs after i, so each quadruplet is reported once.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Split the quadruplet into two pairs, and use a hash map of pair sums seen strictly before index i to avoid duplicates.
slides.narration: Split the quadruplet into two pairs, and use a hash map of pair sums seen strictly before index i to avoid duplicates.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
slides.narration: Four nested loops is n to the fourth. Fixing two and two-pointering the rest is cubic. Storing pair sums in a hash map gives quadratic average time.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. For each i, look at pairs i with j after it and check target minus their sum in the map
2. Then add pairs k with i, k before i, to the map
slides.narration: Step by step. First, for each i, look at pairs i with j after it and check target minus their sum in the map. Second, then add pairs k with i, k before i, to the map. Third, this ordering prevents reusing indices.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: i = 1: look ahead, then store pairs ending at 6
slides.narration: At index 1, value 6: we look for pairs after it whose sum plus a stored earlier pair makes sixteen, finding nothing yet. Then we store every pair that ends at 6.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: i = 2: look ahead, then store pairs ending at 4
slides.narration: At index 2, value 4: we look for pairs after it whose sum plus a stored earlier pair makes sixteen, finding [[7, 6, 4, -1]]. Then we store every pair that ends at 4.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: i = 3: look ahead, then store pairs ending at -1
slides.narration: At index 3, value -1: we look for pairs after it whose sum plus a stored earlier pair makes sixteen, finding nothing yet. Then we store every pair that ends at -1.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: i = 4: look ahead, then store pairs ending at 1
slides.narration: At index 4, value 1: we look for pairs after it whose sum plus a stored earlier pair makes sixteen, finding [[7, 6, 1, 2]]. Then we store every pair that ends at 1.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: For each i from one, we look at every j after i and add each stored pair summing to target minus a i minus a j. Then we store all pairs of earlier elements with a i.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n squared avg. Space is O of n squared.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Only store pairs *before* i to avoid reusing elements
Worst case O(n³) when many pairs share a sum
slides.narration: Add pairs ending at i only after looking ahead from i, so the two halves never overlap and each quadruplet is found once.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: The ordering trick is the heart of the solution; explain it. The k-sum generalisation recurses down to two-sum.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Split the quadruplet into two pairs, and use a hash map of pair sums seen strictly before index i to avoid duplicates.
slides.narration: To recap Four Number Sum: Split the quadruplet into two pairs, and use a hash map of pair sums seen strictly before index i to avoid duplicates. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
